body.text: On November 15, Philippine Foreign Secretary Theresa Lazaro announced that ASEAN countries and China had reached provisional agreement on about 80 percent of the paragraphs in the draft Code of Conduct on the South China Sea (COC), while conceding that Manila would not meet its goal of concluding the negotiations this year. Lazaro’s remark that the Philippines would “leave this almost 80 percent finished document to Singapore” just indicates both the progress made and the challenge ahead.

The 80 percent figure refers to paragraphs in the draft text that have received provisional agreement. There may be just one-fifth of the text left to finalize, but it’s the hardest part. Some of the most consequential questions are still outstanding, like the geographical scope of the COC and whether it will carry legally binding force. These issues go to the heart of what the agreement will cover, whom it will govern, and how much practical authority it will carry.

The Philippines has nevertheless given Singapore a strong foundation to work on. ASEAN and China held nine rounds of negotiations and two senior officials’ meetings in 2026. Those talks managed to raise the amount of paragraphs under provisional agreement from approximately 50 percent to 80 percent. They also reached a preliminary understanding on the relationship between the 2002 Declaration on the Conduct of Parties in the South China Sea (DOC) and the future COC, agreeing that the former would provide the foundation for the latter. The COC is now being envisioned as a platform for practical maritime cooperation and a mechanism for managing differences at sea.

Yet, the progress so far has yet to translate into a common ASEAN position on what the COC should ultimately cover and achieve. The Philippines and Vietnam are directly involved in maritime disputes with China, while Malaysia and Brunei have their own maritime interests and concerns over offshore resources, alongside distinct approaches to managing relations with Beijing. Indonesia, although not a claimant to any disputed reefs or islands, has also experienced tensions with China over maritime rights in the waters north of the Natuna Islands. Other states, like Cambodia, Laos, and Thailand, have no direct stake in the South China Sea.

These differences shape member states’ preferences regarding the COC’s geographical scope, legal obligations, and implementation. Singapore’s task in 2027 will therefore be to help ASEAN reconcile these differing priorities and sustain a sufficiently coherent position in its negotiations with China.

Against this backdrop, Singapore’s own position is worth examining. As a non-claimant state, Singapore does not take sides on the competing territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea. It does, however, have substantial interests in the matter. As a small, trade-dependent nation, Singapore relies on regional peace and stability, freedom of navigation and overflight, and the peaceful resolution of disputes in accordance with international law, including the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). This combination of a non-claimant position and a strong commitment to international law gives Singapore a distinct perspective on the COC. Its priority is to help establish a credible regional framework that can manage maritime tensions, preserve freedom of navigation, and safeguard the rights and interests of all parties.

Singapore’s diplomatic positioning also provides an important foundation for this role. It has a long-standing relationship with China, underpinned by extensive economic ties, regular high-level exchanges, and institutionalized bilateral cooperation. In 2023, the two countries upgraded their relationship to an “All-Round High-Quality Future-Oriented Partnership.” Meanwhile, Singapore has consistently regarded ASEAN as a central platform for engaging major powers and safeguarding the interests of smaller states. This combination gives Singapore established channels for communications with Beijing while allowing it to advance the COC through an ASEAN-led framework. However, close bilateral relations do not automatically translate into greater bargaining leverage, just as Singapore’s non-claimant status does not make it a neutral observer of the principles at stake.

Under Article 32 of the ASEAN Charter, the chair is tasked with advancing ASEAN’s interests through policy initiatives, coordination, consensus-building, and cooperation, as well as providing good offices when urgent regional issues arise. These responsibilities give Singapore considerable influence over agenda-setting, diplomatic coordination and the pace of negotiations. That said, substantive decisions within ASEAN remain governed by the principles of consultation and consensus, as stipulated in Article 20 of the Charter. Singapore must therefore secure the support of its fellow member states before advancing a common position in negotiations with China. The outcome will also depend on Beijing’s willingness to accommodate ASEAN’s expectations. The chair can narrow differences and sustain momentum but cannot substitute for the political compromises required from all parties.

Lazaro’s assessment that negotiations could be completed within another five to six months offers grounds for optimism, but Singapore should resist allowing the pressure of a deadline to overshadow the more fundamental objective of securing an effective and substantive agreement. A hastily concluded COC that leaves critical provisions open to competing interpretations would do little to address the underlying challenges in the South China Sea. The last 20 percent will matter far more than its numerical share suggests.

For Singapore, the challenge is not simply to bring a long-delayed negotiation across the finish line, but to help transform more than two decades of diplomatic efforts into a meaningful and practical regional framework.
